Flagellate

FLAJ-uh-layt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To flagellate to whip or flog, often as punishment or penance.

Medieval accounts describe certain religious orders choosing to flagellate themselves as an act of devotion.

Worked Example

The drill sergeant's insults felt almost designed to flagellate the recruits' confidence rather than build it.

The insults weren't physical, but they battered the recruits' morale just as harshly as a whip would -- a non-literal extension of flagellate.

How Flagellate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

flog

flog: beat someone as a punishment

scourge

Antonyms

pamper

pamper: treat someone with special kindness and comfort

How Strong Is It? — spank → flagellate → torture

spank vs. flagellate

spank vs. flagellate: A spank is a single light strike, often disciplinary; flagellate implies a repeated, severe whipping.

torture vs. flagellate

torture vs. flagellate: Flagellate is one specific method of physical punishment; torture is the broader, more extreme category it belongs to.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — flagell

root — flagell: whip (Latin (flagellum))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or perform an action (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Flagellate comes directly from Latin flagellum, 'a whip,' plus -ate -- so flagellate literally means 'to whip.'

Use the root in a new word: flagellum

Use the root in a new word: flagellum: The same root survives untouched in biology's flagellum, the whip-like tail some bacteria and sperm cells use to swim.

Root Check

Word Choice

Flagellate is often used in a non-literal sense today ("self-flagellate") for someone punishing themselves emotionally over guilt or failure, more often than for literal whipping.
